A comprehensive explanation of our approach, dubbed 'Circuit-Target', has been documented in this paper. Firstly, we devised a novel benchmark consisting of 500 accurate representations of 9-input combinatorial total functions. This benchmark served as the basis for evaluating our proposed method, which employs genetic evolution to evolve combinatorial circuits. A key innovation in Circuit-Target involves the utilization of gradient-based optimization, which enables the circuit's weights to be adjusted during the evolution process. Empirical evidence confirms that Circuit-Target outperforms existing methods, yielding 95% accuracy on the aforementioned benchmark. Furthermore, we provide insight into four distinct evaluation strategies, which suggest that our approach excels even against competitors that cheat by utilizing additional information. Ultimately, the paper provides anecdotal evidence suggesting that Circuit-Target can successfully generalize to larger input lengths.

nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, where the weight between two neurons increases if their spike times synchronize and decreases if their spike times become desynchronized. Our research reveals that MPN possesses two critical properties essential for effective sequence learning. First, any given sequence can be learned by initializing the network appropriately. Secondly, the model exhibits asymptotic stability, meaning the spike times of neurons converge to the desired pattern over time. Furthermore, our mathematical analysis demonstrates that MPN can accurately predict the temporal structure of learned sequences, yielding precise estimates as time approaches infinity. To evaluate the model's validity, numerical simulations of MPN's behavior were performed. Our results confirm that MPN is capable of robust and long-term sequence learning, often resisting distractions and maintaining the core temporal structure of the target sequence even in presence of irrelevant stimuli.

This study introduces a method for generating chaos expansions of random right-hand sides in specific types of differential equations, which proves to be highly efficient. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and the complexity of the environments in which they operate. Moreover, industrial settings tend to experience changes that affect measurement data, such as variations in production rates or quality control processes. This problem is further compounded in distributed manufacturing scenarios, where the challenge of collaborative multi-source state estimation is amplified across networked systems. This work presents a new approach to address these difficulties, focusing on the development of novel algorithms for data reduction and filtering in the presence of time-varying phenomena and network disruptions. This approach is evaluated through the implementation of a distributed fault detection, data reconstruction, and control design framework known as Distributed Fault Detection and Reconstruction using a Decentralized Algorithm (DFDRA-DA). DFDRA-DA is utilized in a realistic manufacturing scenario to demonstrate its effectiveness in handling real-world data and network dynamics. This approach is further extended to accommodate communication constraints and network disruptions while allowing for decentralized decision-making. This capability is leveraged to design an optimized batch control system that complements the decentralized estimation algorithm and enables efficient operation across networked systems. This work also presents an open-source simulation platform known as the Manufacturing Scenario Simulator (MSS). The MSS is designed to facilitate the evaluation of control strategies in diverse manufacturing scenarios, providing the ability to introduce failures and varying conditions for more comprehensive testing.

By stacking similar data together, our analysis covered the entire evolutionary period of both galaxy systems, from their initial formation to their merger with the Milky Way.

The Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems originated from primordial gas and dark matter cores that formed specifically suited to create long-gaunted stellar halo structures, typically found in massive galaxy systems. 

Our model indicates that these galaxy cores grew surrounded by extensive, thinly spread gas layers, which later transformed into extended halo structures that reach far beyond the original disk distributions. 

Our analysis, based on comprehensive data patterns, shows a significant correspondence between these galaxy systems and "in-situ" star clusters formed within the original halo, producing ancient 12 billion-year-old star groups, such as the Virgo giant globular cluster, NGC 4557.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and comprehensive analysis. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy high-accuracy and fast-pruned models directly without additional overhead compared to traditional methods, while also minimizing the pruning-after-training approach by up to 2 times with comparable results.

avitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation from the same sources offers a vast array of opportunities for multi-messenger research. Nonetheless, the majority of gravitational waves generated by neutron star mergers are too faint to be detected by current detectors, and therefore an advanced detector with greater sensitivity in the low-frequency range is essential. A next-generation detector, which is now under development, will ultimately facilitate the detection of such events. This study examines the potential for using ultra-short pulse signals to characterize the stochastic gravitational wave background generated by neutron star mergers based on earlier observations of binary neutron star mergers and gamma-ray bursts. Signals of this type are too brief for current detectors, but a next-generation detector with greater sensitivity in the low-frequency range will ultimately be required to detect such events.

giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by remaining in its original location rather than being formed by a specific high-energy migration mechanism. Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully apply our algorithm to critical problems with such a structure: multi-product inventory control with a limited capacity and production planning under a capacity constraint. Our simulation results illustrate that our algorithm enables effective exploration of these large CMDPs.

Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism-based approach, similar to other methods in this category, returns a conservative treatment policy that guarantees optimality in some optimal dynamic treatment regime when there's limited data available for each state. Current pessimism-based methods are limited in that they don't generalise state-action combinations and therefore can be inefficient when dealing with large datasets. A new pessimism-based algorithm that addresses these shortcomings is introduced, which uses a pessimistic Bayesian posterior belief update based on an exploratory empirical distribution. This belief update ensures that the optimal dynamic treatment regime's execution is both conservative and generalizes state-action combinations. Moreover, we propose a new pessimism-based algorithm that estimates a conservative upper bound on the Bayesian optimal dynamic treatment regime's performance. This performance bound is guaranteed to increase as the amount of data in the empirical distribution grows. The effectiveness of these algorithms is demonstrated in both simulation-based testing and the analysis of a real-world medical dataset.

These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses investigating the regional distribution of languages. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically clustered languages, detection of overlapping patterns, and revealing known or unknown multi-regional language distributions. However, evaluating the quality of these clusters proves challenging due to the cluster-assigned labels being uncertain and the absence of clear cluster boundaries in presence-absence data. To address this issue, a novel framework has been developed to quantify the quality of these clusters by assigning a cluster-related score to each data point, which measures how confidently associated a presence-absence pattern is with a particular cluster. This framework utilizes Bayesian non-parametric binary mixture models to find the optimal number of clusters and characterizes the uncertainty associated with each data point's cluster assignment. Ultimately, a case study involving the analysis of German dialects in Switzerland showcases the effectiveness of this framework in clustering presence-absence data.

deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs in a cross-attention manner, our model can effectively learn essential features and attain improved performance. This novel approach yields superior results for RGB and RGB-D image challenging datasets.

2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro average F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro average F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

Since X-rays pass through matter at varying rates, the process produces images that distinguish between different materials by measuring X-ray absorption levels. Modern CT systems employ high-energy, highly focused X-ray beams that cover a range of wavelengths, prompting concerns about their potential effects on biological specimens. This has sparked a desire to analyze speciemens under both scanned and unscanned states to investigate changes caused by the scanning process. To address this issue, a new technique called label-free fluorescence microscopy aims to observe the specimen's internal structures within the scanned area. To achieve this, the technique relies on detecting slight changes in the specimen's structure that respond to X-rays by emitting visible light. To facilitate this detection, specialized microscopes are used to observe both stained and unscained specimens alongside scanned and unscanned specimens, allowing the collection of comparative data. To implement this approach, a custom-built, high-resolution X-ray source employs a unique transmission-mode microfocus seal to increase the visibility of internal structures and optimize scanning conditions. Preliminary results from experiments conducted using this setup demonstrate the potential of this technique to provide high-resolution images of microscopic structures within biological specimens using both scanned and unscanned states.

A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for the expensive annotation process. , has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications have now successfully adopted traditional procedural programming techniques.  This paper presents the results of a case study that involved rewriting and benchmarking a series of vector operations using both procedural and object-oriented programming techniques.  Our findings indicate that, despite initial expectations that object-oriented programming would result in a notable performance improvement, the actual outcome was a modest decline in memory by 20-30% and processing time by 10-30% when compared to procedural programming in certain scenarios.  Our research highlights the potential for object-oriented programming to generate inefficient GPU code, potentially limiting its effectiveness in high-performance computing environments.

Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with restrictions. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to the circuit's size, and our experiments demonstrate that this bound is usually precise, and our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of efficiency.

By deriving an effective Hamiltonian, the evolution of the impurity oscillations can be understood as a periodic rotation of the spin-orbit field, resulting in oscillations with frequencies proportional to the acceleration, much like simple harmonic motion. This regime, dominated by oscillations, can persist even at accelerated speeds where de Broglie wave interference leads to wave packet revivals. Moreover, the presence of spin-orbit coupling extends the validity of this oscillatory regime to higher acceleration levels.

The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, the code is a partial ovoid or partial spread; a code is full if it meets all these criteria. A set of codes in a generalized quadrangle is an ovoid spectrum if all codes in the set are full and have the same minimum distance. In this paper, we introduce a new aspect to the ovoid spectrum by considering spreads and ovoids as both would remain unchanged under the codes' transformation. The paper then presents an ovoid spectrum containing spreads and ovoids for the first time in a classical generalized quadrangle, specifically in its second order.

the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, we found that gas density in the CMZ is significantly influenced by anisotropic spatial patterns at a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. , femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the course of the pulse. The use of X-ray pulse linear polarization significantly enhances the possibilities for studying highly excited solid-state physics by enabling analysis of specific spin-orbit coupled transitions. A specific class of materials known as 2D materials possesses inherent spin-orbit coupling, resulting in unique valence band structures near the Fermi level. By combining the incredibly high peak power of X-ray free-electron lasers with the unique properties of spin-orbit coupled 2D semiconductors, researchers open themselves up to an expanded understanding of ultrafast X-ray spectroscopy techniques, among other advancements. To study this phenomenon, X-ray pulse nonlinear spectroscopies such as X-ray pulse resonant inelastic scattering, X-ray pulse resonant photo-ejection spectroscopy, and X-ray pulse nonlinear absorption coefficients can be employed. Byporting these X-ray pulse nonlinear spectroscopy findings, researchers can develop a comprehensive picture of highly excited 2D spin-orbit coupled states.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is presented to create entangled states of polarized light without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By employing the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entangled photons, known as polarization-identified photons, it is possible to create the desired entangled states while maintaining control over their degree of entanglement. This process can be performed repeatedly without damaging the underlying quantum state, making it suitable for various applications in quantum information processing. Furthermore, a hybrid approach is proposed for generating hyperentangled states, which could greatly expand the range of applications due to its ability to leverage both spontaneous parametric down conversion and entanglement of identical photons.

Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this study proposes adopting multiple loss measures according to device misidentification rates, thus introducing the concept of risk in IoT device classification. This is formulated as a combinatorial optimization issue and resolved using the CE stochastic optimization strategy, a novel algorithm presented in this paper. Using real-world traffic, the efficacy of the approach in choosing the optimal features to minimize misidentification risks within specific feature extraction cost limits is illustrated.

an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel modal algebras and their corresponding relational structures, specifically the respective modal logic systems. These investigations mimic a previous study on intutionistic modal logics. The main goal is to identify the variety of basic Godel modal algebras that correspond to the Godel version of the intutionistic modal logic S4MI. This study demonstrates that the variety of basic Godel modal algebras for S4MI is the variety defined by the Burroni algebra with the Smiley axiom, and it also identifies the relational structures that correspond to this variety. The research also identifies the varieties of basic Godel modal algebras for other subvarieties of normal modal logics within the intutionistic framework.

If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. With a specified mean PBH mass, our analysis suggests that primordial black holes could produce about 4 times more microlensing events than stellar black holes. Our study predicts that a planned astronomical survey will likely detect a thousand times the number of these hypothetical black hole-related microlensing events.

We simulated a wide range of concentrations of molecules in various fluids and observed the resulting phase behavior. It was found that a particular range of concentrations resulted in systems where the individual molecules occupied distinct areas on the surface. Additionally, when the concentration of molecules exceeded this specific range, the liquid crystalline phase became more stable than the fluid phase, displaying characteristics similar to those seen in systems consisting of rod-shaped molecules. Further examination revealed that the shapes of the liquid-to-liquid phase transition curves varied depending on the size of the molecules. It was observed that wider ranges of concentrations favor the formation of the liquid crystalline phase. Moreover, when the concentration of molecules was extremely high, the typical gap between the fluid and liquid crystalline phases disappeared and the system entered a more concentrated range, resulting in a system where the individual molecules occupied distinct areas on the surface. Our simulations provided essential insights into how the characteristics of the molecules affect these phases and suggested the creation of a system where one can manipulate the liquid crystalline phase using variations in concentration of molecules.

The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. However, quantum researchers have devised a variant of this setup in which the subject does not interact with the light. Instead, a measurement is conducted on the free-propagating photons. This modified setup has enabled the development of quantum and classical imaging techniques that transcend the standard diffraction limit. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions.

To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the Higgs boson. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to the masses of sub-GeV dark matter particles, with proposed future experiments having the potential to explore a range of dark matter masses that are currently out of reach.

These magnetic bright points have the same size as the resolution of the observations and are found both individually and in large groups. In this paper, we examine the properties of magnetic bright points in different locations on the solar surface using data from the High Resolution Telescope and Instrument, which operates on the High Resolution Imaging Camera for the Sun, a solar observatory in space. We look at their size, movement, and variations in density and temperature, and find that their properties in areas with and without sunspots are similar, with some differences in density and temperature patterns. In areas with sunspots, a pattern of magnetic bright points forms a series of connected dots, or "sea of dots", with the density of the magnetic bright points decreasing towards the sunspots and changing in temperature in a specific direction. We explore how these magnetic bright points in the solar atmosphere behave in response to the dynamic movement of the solar surface and the formation of solar granules, which are natural patterns in the solar photosphere.

we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern.

rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling with benchmarking to capture a broader, more accurate picture of each model's performance across the full dataset. To achieve this, we propose a multi-stage benchmarking process, involving dataset sub-sampling and efficient, heuristic-based model evaluations, both within an algorithm's iterative optimization and external to it. By optimizing these sub-samples to represent the dataset in a way that is informative about each model's performance, we ensure that our benchmarking results are both excludating any potential biases and encompassing a broader range of models. Furthermore, we aim to develop a dynamic dataset representation that can adapt to each model's requirements, enabling profiling that is both independent of the model and capable of identifying dataset features critical to its performance.

One of its key attributes is its ability to simulate any CPT-computable choice of functions efficiently. However, there is an ongoing uncertainty regarding the computational efficiency of a specific task - determining whether a CPT-computable choice of functions is computable in PTIME. This issue has led to doubting the theoretical superiority of CPT over PTIME, with some experts considering PTIME as an equally fundamental concept. Yet, a fundamental difference exists - PTIME is characterized by a fixed number of variables, limiting its computational scope, whereas CPT can handle an arbitrarily large number of variables. This paper presents a significant breakthrough in CPT theory, providing an explicit upper limit on the number of computable choices that CPT can efficiently handle. One of the most notable findings from this research is the proof that a previously defined variant of CPT, called constant-time CPT, has the ability to efficiently handle an exponentially large number of variables, significantly surpassing previous machine models. Additionally, this study provides a thorough comparison of constant-time CPT and PTIME, establishing a computationally efficient relationship and highlighting their combined computational strength. Lastly, this research proves that there is an inherent separation between constant-time CPT and a related machine model, known as tally PTIME, based on a fundamental problem

To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. We investigate the broader idea of'maximally cyclic' numbers, defining them as the maximum value that can be achieved for the $k$-th term of a cyclic sequence of length $n$. By analyzing both the natural numbers and the real numbers in intervals [0,1], we find that'maximally cyclic' natural numbers and'maximally cyclic' real numbers in intervals [0,1] equal $n-1$.

However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have shown significant interest in removing such noise and extracting precise IBIs from contaminated signals. This task can be approached as a de-noising problem and solved using non-local means filters. By applying a non-local means-based de-noising technique to 2D vector ECG signals, you can effectively remove motion noise and accurately identify IBIs. This method uses a generalized non-local means framework that incorporates vector data and is successfully demonstrated on 2D vector ECG signals captured by chest accelerometers and surface ECG signals captured by wearable devices.

Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision.

This scenario involves navigating unfamiliar environments with unfamiliar landmarks referenced through brief video sequences.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish two primary contributions in this research area. Firstly, a tight bound is derived for how much information this adversary can gain, relating to the difficulty of determining the smallest confusion graph that matches the given source entropy. Secondly, a tighter bound is derived for a more nuanced adversary scenario, where the adversary can take multiple guesses and are allowed to slightly err in their guesses, reflecting a scenario where the adversary is allowed a small amount of leakage.

(2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "Q-learning" framework based on the q-function, separate from time-discretized Q-learning. This approach yields a SARSA-type algorithm, which can be applied to various environments, including those with continuous action spaces, using stochastic approximation equations. We apply this algorithm in examples involving: (i) a 1D normal distribution, where simulation results show its performance compared to time-discretized Q-learning; (ii) a 2D rotation matrix, where simulation results demonstrate its capability in handling continuous action spaces; and (iii) a CAT model, where we analyze the relationship between risk-neutral and risk-averse behaviors under "Q-learning".

influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were preoccupied with advancing actual scientific work.
